title: Why High School 'Rigor' Is Often Just a Facade
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler argues that rising high school transcripts, with tougher courses, more credits and higher GPAs, mask flat science scores and declining math scores on NAEP. She dismisses grade inflation and equity pressures as the whole explanation and says the deeper cause is an elementary and middle school curriculum that never gives students the knowledge high school work assumes. A pseudonymous English teacher's knowledge tests, in which freshmen cannot name five European countries, serve as the anecdotal evidence, and the problem is shown to reach affluent schools as well as high-poverty ones. She rejects blaming phones or lower-grade teachers and treats soft skills as no substitute for content. Her remedy is a content-rich elementary curriculum in history, science and the arts, plus teacher training in how long-term memory works, with high school teachers meanwhile filling gaps explicitly.
points: Course labels, credits and GPAs have risen while NAEP-linked math and science results have not, so transcript rigor is a poor proxy for learning.
Grade inflation is only part of the story; the root cause is a thin elementary curriculum that leaves students without the background knowledge high school texts assume.
The knowledge deficit appears in wealthy schools too, where students stay silent in class because they know how much they do not know.
Emphasising higher-order thinking skills over content leaves students with no bricks to build with, and Wexler ties this to student anxiety.
The fix is knowledge-building curricula from kindergarten, and in the short term explicit, sequenced writing activities that fill gaps.
quotes: A recently released federal study analyzed high school transcripts from a representative sample of high school graduates in the class of 2019. As compared to their peers ten years before, this group took tougher courses, earned more credits overall, and had higher GPAs—all of which sounds like real progress.

But when researchers linked grades in math and science courses to scores on standardized tests in those subjects given as part of the National Assessment of Educational Progress, or NAEP, they found something disturbing. Science scores were flat and math scores actually declined, even for students taking more rigorous courses.

But while “soft skills” like perseverance are important, they’re not a substitute for learning; students need both. And it’s great to boost students’ confidence, but only if you’re also giving them a solid basis for that confidence. Otherwise, they’re likely to discover at some point—in college, or on the job—that they lack the knowledge or skills that are expected, and their confidence will crumble.

Many students don’t learn much history or science before high school, either because it simply isn’t taught, or because it isn’t taught in a way that will stick. All of these possible problems stem from a disconnect between teacher training and materials, on the one hand, and what science has discovered about how people learn, on the other.

Smith believes students are suffering from the system’s failure to provide them with access to knowledge. She says they’re reluctant to volunteer information in class because they’re aware of how much they don’t know and they “don’t want to look stupid.

This group of kids has grown up 'thinking deeply,'” she wrote in her email. “However, they have not been given the bricks of knowledge required to build the houses of thinking. Can you imagine being asked to build and build and build without any materials?

But the most effective solution to this problem is to inject more content into the elementary curriculum—history, science, the arts—and to educate teachers at all grade levels about the importance of storing information in long-term memory.
